quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-01.title: Counting cycles and Sylow normalizers
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-01.body:
**(a)** An element of order $7$ in $S_7$ has cycle lengths with lcm $7$, so it is a $7$-cycle. The number of $7$-cycles is $7!/7=6!=720$. All $7$-cycles are conjugate in $S_7$, so for a $7$-cycle $\sigma$, $|C_{S_7}(\sigma)|=|S_7|/720=5040/720=7$ (indeed $C_{S_7}(\sigma)=\langle\sigma\rangle$).

**(b)** A Sylow $7$-subgroup of $S_7$ or $A_7$ has order $7$ and contains $6$ seven-cycles, and distinct ones intersect trivially; so there are $720/6=120$ of them. Since $7$-cycles are even, these are exactly the Sylow $7$-subgroups of $A_7$, and they are all conjugate in $A_7$ (Sylow). Hence
$$|N_{A_7}(P)|=\frac{|A_7|}{120}=\frac{2520}{120}=21.$$
(Concretely, $N_{S_7}(P)\cong C_7\rtimes C_6$ of order $42$, and the $C_6$, generated by $x\mapsto 3x$ on $\mathbb Z/7$, is a $6$-cycle, which is odd.)

**(c)** Suppose $G\le S_7$ is simple of order $504$. If $G\not\le A_7$ then $G\cap A_7$ is a normal subgroup of index $2$, contradicting simplicity; so $G\le A_7$. In $G$, $n_7(G)\equiv1\pmod7$ divides $72$, so $n_7(G)\in\{1,8,36\}$, and $n_7(G)\ne1$ by simplicity. For $P\in\mathrm{Syl}_7(G)$ we get $|N_G(P)|=504/n_7(G)\in\{63,14\}$. But $P$ is also a Sylow $7$-subgroup of $A_7$, and $N_G(P)\le N_{A_7}(P)$, so $|N_G(P)|$ divides $21$ by (b). Neither $63$ nor $14$ divides $21$ — contradiction. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-02.title: Clearing denominators
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-02.body:
**(a)** Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be a $K$-basis of $E$. Each $e=e_i$ is algebraic over $K$; clearing denominators in a polynomial relation gives $a_de^d+a_{d-1}e^{d-1}+\cdots+a_0=0$ with $a_j\in R$, $a_d\ne0$. Multiplying by $a_d^{d-1}$:
$$(a_de)^d+a_{d-1}(a_de)^{d-1}+a_{d-2}a_d(a_de)^{d-2}+\cdots+a_0a_d^{d-1}=0,$$
so $x_i=a_de_i$ is integral over $R$. The $x_i$ still form a $K$-basis of $E$ since $a_d\ne0$.

Let $S=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]\subseteq E$. If $x_i$ satisfies a monic equation of degree $d_i$ over $R$, then every power $x_i^k$ is an $R$-combination of $1,x_i,\dots,x_i^{d_i-1}$, so $S$ is generated as an $R$-module by the finitely many monomials $x_1^{k_1}\cdots x_n^{k_n}$ with $0\le k_i<d_i$.

The field of fractions $\operatorname{Frac}(S)$ (taken inside the field $E$) contains $R$, hence $\operatorname{Frac}(R)=K$, and contains the $x_i$, hence their $K$-span $E$. So $\operatorname{Frac}(S)=E$.

**(b)** Let $L\supseteq E$ be a splitting field of $f$ over $E$ and write $f=\prod_{i=1}^d(X-\alpha_i)$ in $L[X]$, $\alpha_1=\alpha$. Let $g\in R[X]$ be monic with $g(\alpha)=0$. Since $f$ is irreducible over $K$, for each $i$ there is a $K$-isomorphism $K(\alpha)\to K(\alpha_i)$, $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_i$; it fixes the coefficients of $g$, so $g(\alpha_i)=0$. Thus each $\alpha_i$ is integral over $R$. The coefficients of $f$ are, up to sign, elementary symmetric polynomials in the $\alpha_i$; since integral elements form a ring, they are integral over $R$. They lie in $K$, and $R$ is integrally closed in $K$, so they lie in $R$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-03.title: Factoring $X^{q^n}-X$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-03.body:
$|E|=q^n$ and $E^\times$ has order $q^n-1$, so every $e\in E$ satisfies $e^{q^n}=e$; hence $X^{q^n}-X=\prod_{e\in E}(X-e)$.

**(a)** Let $g\in F[X]$ be monic irreducible of degree $d\mid n$, and let $\theta$ be a root of $g$ in some extension. Then $F(\theta)$ is a field with $q^d$ elements, so $\theta^{q^d}=\theta$; iterating $n/d$ times, $\theta^{q^n}=\theta$. As $g$ is the minimal polynomial of $\theta$, $g\mid X^{q^n}-X=\prod_{e\in E}(X-e)$. So $g$ has a root $e\in E$, and being monic irreducible, $g$ is the minimal polynomial of $e$ over $F$.

**(b)** $h=X^{q^n}-X$ is separable ($h'=-1$), so it is the product of distinct monic irreducible factors. Each irreducible factor is the minimal polynomial of some $e\in E$, of degree $[F(e):F]$, which divides $[E:F]=n$. Conversely by (a) every monic irreducible of degree dividing $n$ divides $h$. Therefore
$$\prod_{\substack{g\text{ monic irred.}\\ \deg g\mid n}}g=X^{q^n}-X.$$

**(c)** Let $N_d$ be the number of monic irreducibles of degree $d$ over $GF(2)$. Comparing degrees in (b): $\sum_{d\mid n}dN_d=2^n$.
- $n=1$: $N_1=2$.
- $n=2$: $N_1+2N_2=4$, so $N_2=1$.
- $n=5$: $N_1+5N_5=32$, so $N_5=6$.
- $n=10$: $N_1+2N_2+5N_5+10N_{10}=1024$, i.e. $2+2+30+10N_{10}=1024$, so $N_{10}=99$.

(Möbius inversion gives the same: $N_{10}=\frac1{10}(2^{10}-2^5-2^2+2^1)=\frac{990}{10}=99$.)

**Answer: (b) $X^{q^n}-X$; (c) $99$.** ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-04.title: Invariant subspaces and cyclic vectors
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-04.body:
Assume $V\ne0$, $n=\dim V$.

**(a)** ($\Rightarrow$) Let $W$ be a $T$-invariant subspace with $0<\dim W=k<n$. Extending a basis of $W$ to $V$, the matrix of $T$ is block triangular $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&C\end{pmatrix}$ with $A$ the matrix of $T|_W$, so $f=f_A\,f_C$ with $\deg f_A=k$, $\deg f_C=n-k$, both positive. So $f$ is reducible.

($\Leftarrow$) Suppose there is no proper nonzero invariant subspace. Take $v\ne0$; the cyclic subspace $\langle v,Tv,T^2v,\dots\rangle$ is invariant and nonzero, so it is $V$. If $T^kv$ were a combination of $v,\dots,T^{k-1}v$ for some $k<n$, then the span of $v,\dots,T^{k-1}v$ would be invariant and equal to the cyclic subspace, of dimension $<n$; so $v,Tv,\dots,T^{n-1}v$ are independent. Hence no nonzero polynomial of degree $<n$ annihilates $T$.

Now suppose $f=gh$ with $g,h$ monic of positive degree (so both degrees are $<n$). Let $W=\ker g(T)$, which is $T$-invariant. $W\ne V$ because $g(T)\ne0$. $W\ne0$: by Cayley–Hamilton $g(T)h(T)=f(T)=0$, and $h(T)\ne0$, so $0\ne h(T)V\subseteq\ker g(T)$. This contradicts the hypothesis; hence $f$ is irreducible.

**(b)** Since $f$ is irreducible and $\operatorname{char}F=0$, $f'\ne0$ has smaller degree, so $\gcd(f,f')=1$ and $f$ is separable: it has $n$ distinct roots $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ in the algebraic closure $\bar F$. Over $\bar F$, $T$ therefore has $n$ distinct eigenvalues; eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so they form a basis of $\bar F\otimes_FV$, and $T$ is diagonalizable over $\bar F$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-05.title: Composition series of $R_R$
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2010s-05.body:
**(a)** Let $i$ be the least index with $I_i\not\subseteq M$ (it exists as $I_n=R$). Then $I_{i-1}\subseteq M$, and $I_i+M=R$ by maximality of $M$. So
$$R/M=(I_i+M)/M\cong I_i/(I_i\cap M).$$
Now $I_{i-1}\subseteq I_i\cap M\subsetneq I_i$, and $I_i/I_{i-1}$ is simple, so $I_i\cap M=I_{i-1}$ and $R/M\cong V_i$.

**(b)** *Lemma.* If $W_1,\dots,W_n$ are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules and $X\subseteq W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_n$ projects onto each $W_i$, then $X$ is everything. (Induction: the projection $\rho$ of $X$ to $W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_{n-1}$ is onto by induction. If $X\cap W_n=W_n$, then $X=\rho(X)\oplus W_n$. If $X\cap W_n=0$, $\rho$ is injective and $\pi_n\rho^{-1}$ is a surjection $W_1\oplus\cdots\oplus W_{n-1}\to W_n$ that vanishes on each $W_i$ by Schur's lemma, since $W_i\not\cong W_n$ — impossible.)

Choose $0\ne v_i\in V_i$ and define $\phi\colon R\to V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$, $\phi(r)=(v_1r,\dots,v_nr)$. As $v_iR=V_i$, the lemma shows $\phi$ is onto. Each $\mathrm{ann}(v_i)$ is a maximal right ideal (as $R/\mathrm{ann}(v_i)\cong V_i$ is simple), so the intersection $J$ of all maximal right ideals satisfies $J\subseteq\bigcap_i\mathrm{ann}(v_i)=\ker\phi$. Both $R_R$ and $\bigoplus V_i$ have composition length $n$, so $\ker\phi$ has length $0$: $\ker\phi=0$ and $J=0$.

**(c)** By (b), $\phi\colon R_R\to V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$ is an isomorphism. Left multiplication $r\mapsto\lambda_r$, $\lambda_r(x)=rx$, is a ring isomorphism $R\cong\mathrm{End}_R(R_R)$ (an endomorphism $\psi$ equals $\lambda_{\psi(1)}$). Hence
$$R\cong\mathrm{End}_R\Big(\bigoplus_iV_i\Big)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_R(V_j,V_i)=\prod_{i=1}^n\mathrm{End}_R(V_i),$$
since $\mathrm{Hom}_R(V_j,V_i)=0$ for $i\ne j$ by Schur's lemma and the nonisomorphism hypothesis (the endomorphism ring is "diagonal"). Each $D_i=\mathrm{End}_R(V_i)$ is a division ring by Schur's lemma, so $R\cong D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. (Equivalently, by Wedderburn–Artin $R$ is semisimple, $R\cong\prod M_{n_i}(D_i)$, and each simple module occurs $n_i$ times in $R_R$, so all $n_i=1$.) ∎
